title: The Land in the Days of Joshua

regions.note: The coast and hills from Carmel north toward Sidon (19:24–31).
Upper Galilee, west of the Sea of Chinnereth and the upper Jordan (19:32–39).
Lower Galilee, north of the Jezreel Valley (19:10–16).
The eastern Jezreel Valley and the hills toward the Jordan (19:17–23).
The half-tribe west of the Jordan: the hill country around Shechem north to the Jezreel Valley (17:7–11).
The central hill country from Bethel to Shechem, with Shiloh and Timnath-serah (16:5–10).
The small territory between Judah and Ephraim, from Jericho to Jerusalem, with Gibeon, Ramah and Bethel (18:11–28).

regions.label: Dan
regions.note: First allotted the Shephelah and coast west of Benjamin, with Zorah, Eshtaol and Aijalon (19:40–46); later the tribe moved north to Leshem (19:47).
The largest tribe: the hill country around Hebron, the Shephelah, the Negev and the wilderness by the Salt Sea (15).
Towns within Judah's inheritance in the Negev, around Beersheba (19:1–9).
The plateau east of the Salt Sea, from the Arnon north to Heshbon (13:15–23).
Gilead east of the Jordan, from Heshbon north toward the Sea of Chinnereth (13:24–28).

regions.label: Manasseh
regions.note: The half-tribe east of the Jordan: Bashan and half of Gilead, given by Moses (13:29–31).
The dry south, from Beersheba toward Kadesh-barnea (10:40; 15:21).
The mountains and land north of Israel, part of the land promised (1:4; 13:5–6) but not taken.
The fertile plateau of Og, east of the Sea of Chinnereth, given to the half-tribe of Manasseh (12:4–5; 13:30).
The wooded hill country east of the Jordan, divided between Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh (13:25, 31).
Seir, the hill country south-east of the Salt Sea given to Esau (24:4). Judah's southern border ran along Edom (15:1, 21).
The plateau east of the Salt Sea, south of the Arnon. Balak king of Moab hired Balaam (24:9).
The land of the Ammonites, beyond Gad's eastern border (13:10, 25).

regions.label:
Land of the
Philistines
regions.note: The coast of the five Philistine cities, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron, one of the lands "still to be possessed" (13:2–3).
The rift valley of the Jordan and the Salt Sea and south toward the Red Sea (11:2, 16; 12:1–3).

regions.label: Shephelah
regions.note: The "foothills" (lowland) between the hill country of Judah and the coast (10:40; 15:33).
A small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Chinnereth that Israel did not drive out (13:13).
A small Aramean kingdom below Mount Hermon, not driven out (13:13).
The hill country of Naphtali, where Kedesh was set apart as a city of refuge (20:7).
The broad valley between Galilee and the hill country of Manasseh, where the Canaanites had iron chariots (17:16).
"O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon" (10:12).
Israel crossed it on dry ground opposite Jericho while it overflowed its banks at harvest (3–4). It was the eastern border of the land west of the river.
The Dead Sea, also "the Sea of the Arabah" (3:16), 430 m below sea level.
The Sea of Galilee (12:3; 13:27).
The deep gorge into the Salt Sea, the southern border of the land east of the Jordan (12:1–2; 13:9).
The river (Zarqa) bounding Sihon's kingdom (12:2).

places.note: "The city of Adam, near Zarethan": the waters of the Jordan stood up in a heap here while Israel crossed opposite Jericho (3:16).
The "Ascent of Adummim," the red road climbing from the Jordan Valley toward Jerusalem, on Judah's border (15:7).
"The ruin," east of Bethel. Defeated at first because of Achan's sin, then taken by ambush (7–8). Et-Tell is the usual identification; Khirbet el-Maqatir nearby is another proposal.
"O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon" (10:12). The valley opens west of the Beth-horon pass.
The "Ascent of Scorpions" on Judah's southern border (15:3).
Its king is among the 31 kings defeated (12:14).
One of the five cities of the Philistines; some Anakim remained here, at Gaza and Gath (11:22; 13:3).
One of the five cities of the Philistines (13:3).
With Edrei, a royal city of Og king of Bashan (12:4; 13:12).
On the road down from Beth-horon. The LORD threw down hailstones on the fleeing Amorites "as far as Azekah" (10:10–11).
In the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon: the northern limit of Joshua's conquests (11:17; 12:7).
The southern end of the land; one of the towns of Simeon within Judah (19:2).
At the junction of the Jezreel and Jordan valleys. In Joshua's age an Egyptian garrison town; its Canaanites had iron chariots (17:11, 16).
On Judah's northern border (15:10), a Levitical city (21:16).
Next to Ai (7:2; 8:9), formerly Luz (18:13). Its king is among the defeated (12:16); on the border of Benjamin and Ephraim.
In the wilderness on the plateau, the city of refuge of Reuben (20:8).
Leshem, taken by the tribe of Dan when its land in the south proved too small, and renamed Dan (19:47).
Also Kiriath-sepher, "town of the scroll." Othniel took it and won Caleb's daughter Achsah (15:15–17).
With Ashtaroth, a royal city of Og king of Bashan (12:4).
Its king Debir joined the five kings against Gibeon (10:3); taken in the southern campaign (10:34–35).
One of the five cities of the Philistines (13:3), on Judah's northern border (15:11).
One of the five cities of the Philistines, where Anakim remained (11:22), later the home of Goliath.
The south-west limit of Joshua's campaign (10:41); one of the five Philistine cities left unconquered (13:3).
Its king Horam came to help Lachish and was defeated (10:33), but the Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out (16:10).

places.m: in the region south of Hebron

places.note: The great Hivite city whose people tricked Israel into a treaty (9). When five Amorite kings attacked it, Joshua marched all night from Gilgal; "Sun, stand still over Gibeon" (10:12).
Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, where the twelve stones were set up, the men circumcised and the Passover kept (4:19–5:12). The base of the campaigns until the land was divided at Shiloh.
In Bashan, the northern city of refuge east of the Jordan (20:8).

places.m: in the region between Lachish and Gath

places.note: "The head of all those kingdoms" (11:10). Jabin of Hazor led the northern alliance; Joshua burned the city. The huge mound has a destruction layer with signs of a great fire in the Late Bronze Age.
Also Kiriath-arba, the city of the Anakim. Caleb asked for this hill country at 85 and took it (14:6–15; 15:13–14). A city of refuge (20:7).
The capital of Sihon king of the Amorites, defeated by Moses (12:2; 13:10).
Its king is among the 31 kings defeated (12:14); a town of Simeon (19:4).
Its king Piram joined the five kings against Gibeon (10:3).

The oasis city by its spring, 250 m below sea level, the first city taken west of the Jordan (2; 6). Excavations at Tell es-Sultan have found a long history of walls and destruction; how they fit Joshua 6 is debated, mainly over the date of the conquest.
Jebus, the city of Adoni-zedek, who led the five kings against Gibeon (10:1–5). Its king was defeated, but Judah could not drive out the Jebusites (15:63).
The port at the edge of Dan's territory (19:46).
The oasis from which Moses sent the twelve spies; Caleb recalls it at 85 (14:6–7). The southern limit of Joshua's campaigns (10:41).
Kedesh in Galilee, in the hill country of Naphtali, a city of refuge (20:7).
One of the four Gibeonite cities (9:17), on the border of Judah and Benjamin (15:9).
A great city of the Shephelah, taken in two days in the southern campaign (10:31–32). In the Amarna letters its king wrote to Pharaoh.
Taken in the southern campaign (10:29–30); later a Levitical city (21:13).
The pass of Beth-horon, the road down from the hill country to the Valley of Aijalon, where the Amorites fled from Gibeon (10:10–11).
Jobab king of Madon joined Jabin's northern alliance (11:1).
On the border of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh (13:26, 30); a Levitical city (21:38).
The five Amorite kings hid in the cave here and were brought out and killed (10:16–27).
Guarding the pass into the Jezreel Valley; its king was defeated (12:21), but the Canaanites stayed there (17:11–12).

places.m: the waters of Merom: Ein Meron?
places.note: By "the waters of Merom" the northern kings camped together, and there Joshua fell on them suddenly (11:5–7).
The ridge on Asher's south-western border (19:26); "Jokneam in Carmel" lay at its foot (12:22). (The Carmel of 15:55 is a town in Judah.)

Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal, wrote a copy of the Law on stones, and read the blessings and curses to all Israel (8:30–35). An early Iron Age stone structure on the mountain has been interpreted as this altar.
The mount of blessing, facing Ebal across the valley of Shechem (8:33).
The northern limit of the conquest, "from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon" (11:17); about 2,800 m.
The slopes of Pisgah, from which Moses saw the land (12:3; 13:20; Deuteronomy 34:1).
Ramoth in Gilead, the city of refuge of Gad (20:8).

In the pass between Ebal and Gerizim, a city of refuge (20:7). Here Joshua gathered all the tribes to renew the covenant: "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (24:1, 15); Joseph's bones were buried here (24:32).
The Tabernacle was set up here, and the rest of the land was divided by lot before the LORD (18:1–10). The centre of Israel's worship until the days of Eli and Samuel.
Abel-shittim, Israel's last camp east of the Jordan; from here Joshua sent the two spies to Jericho (2:1; 3:1). Often identified with Tall el-Hammam.
"Greater Sidon" was the limit of the pursuit after the battle at the waters of Merom (11:8).
In the Jordan Valley, given to Gad (13:27).
Joshua's own inheritance in the hill country of Ephraim, where he was buried (19:50; 24:30).
"The fortified city of Tyre" on Asher's border (19:29).
The upper town of the Beth-horon pass, on the border of Ephraim (16:5).
"The Valley of Trouble," where Achan was stoned and a heap of stones raised (7:24–26). Hosea 2:15 promises it will become "a door of hope."
A town of Simeon in the Negev (19:5), later David's base.
Where Moses saw the land and died before Joshua led Israel across (Deuteronomy 34:1–9; Joshua 1:1–2).
A Canaanite city east of the Jordan, Pihilu in the Amarna letters of the 14th century BC.
The great city of Syria (Upi in Egyptian texts) beyond Mount Hermon, not part of the land allotted.
An Egyptian administrative centre in the Valley of Lebanon, known from the Amarna letters.
Bethlehem of Judah is not in the Hebrew list of Judah's towns; the Greek Septuagint includes it with Tekoa (15:59). The Bethlehem of Joshua 19:15 is in Zebulun.

p: Joshua is set at the end of the Late Bronze Age. Canaan was a patchwork of small city-states, each ruled by its own king, such as the 31 kings listed in Joshua 12, and Egypt held the land loosely through garrisons like Beth-shean. In the Amarna letters (about 1350 BC) the kings of Jerusalem, Shechem, Hazor, Lachish and Gezer write to Pharaoh, complaining of one another and of raiders called Habiru.
The date of the conquest is debated: 1 Kings 6:1 points to the 15th century BC, while other scholars prefer the 13th. By about 1208 BC the Merneptah Stele names "Israel" as a people in Canaan.

This map opens from any place named in Joshua, in chapters that have no map of their own. The red dots are places named in Joshua; the black dots are other places of the time, for context. The tribe names show roughly where each tribe's inheritance lay; the maps of Joshua 13–19 draw the allotments.
